title: Very Hot Tea and Coffee Triple Esophageal Cancer Risk, Major Study Finds
excerpt: An Oxford analysis of nearly one million adults found the risk comes from heat itself — not tea or coffee — and that letting a drink cool for a few minutes may prevent a meaningful share of cases.
body:
• People who prefer their tea or coffee "very hot" face roughly three times the risk of developing esophageal squamous cell carcinoma compared with those who drink them "warm," according to a new Oxford study of nearly one million UK adults.
  • Those who like their drinks merely "hot" faced about 1.7 times the risk. Drinking six or more hot beverages a day raised the risk by 71%, regardless of temperature.
  • The link held regardless of smoking, alcohol intake, or whether milk was added — pointing to heat itself, not any ingredient, as the culprit. No link was found for esophageal adenocarcinoma.
  • Researchers estimate about 14% of these cancers could be prevented if "very hot" drinkers switched to "hot." The advice is simple: wait a few minutes before sipping.

The study

Those who enjoy a scalding cup of chai or coffee first thing in the morning may want to wait a few minutes before sipping. Researchers at Oxford Population Health have found that drinking "very hot" beverages is linked to a roughly threefold higher risk of esophageal squamous cell carcinoma (SCC), a type of cancer that forms in the thin, flat cells lining the esophagus.

The analysis combined data from nearly one million adults in two large British cohorts — the Million Women Study and the UK Biobank — making it the largest investigation of its kind to date, according to lead author Keren Papier, a nutritional epidemiologist at Oxford. Participants' self-reported drinking temperatures were tracked against NHS health records over an average of about 14 years in the Million Women Study and 11 years in the UK Biobank. The findings were published in the International Journal of Cancer.

During the follow-up period, 2,348 participants developed esophageal cancer: 1,045 cases of SCC and 1,303 of adenocarcinoma. When the researchers separated the two types, the difference was stark.

What the numbers show

Compared with people who reported drinking their beverages "warm," those who drank them "hot" had around 1.7 times the risk of SCC, while those who drank them "very hot" had around a three times higher risk — a pooled relative risk of 3.17, or a 217% increase. The pattern held steady across the board: hotter beverages were associated with progressively higher risk.

Volume mattered too. Participants who drank six or more hot drinks daily faced a 71% higher risk of SCC than those who drank fewer than six, even after accounting for drink temperature. It made no difference whether people primarily drank tea or coffee, suggesting the risk came from the temperature of the liquid rather than any specific ingredient.

"This large study provides robust evidence that drink temperature as well as frequency of hot drink consumption are likely to be substantial risk factors for SCC," the study authors wrote.

It's the heat, not the chai

Crucially, the increased risk held regardless of smoking status, alcohol intake, or whether milk was added to the drinks — factors that often confound cancer studies. The risk applies to the temperature of the drink and not the drink itself. A "very hot" beverage is approximately 149 degrees Fahrenheit, whereas a "hot" drink is about 140 degrees, though in this study temperatures were self-reported rather than directly measured — the researchers' main acknowledged limitation, since heat tolerance varies between people.

There was also reassuring nuance: neither temperature nor volume was meaningfully linked to esophageal adenocarcinoma, the other major type of esophageal cancer, where the risk stayed about the same regardless of how people drank.

"While the risk of being diagnosed with this cancer remains relatively low in the UK, this research does add to the evidence that drinking very hot drinks could increase the risk of esophageal squamous cell carcinoma. There is, however, a simple step people can take: let a cuppa cool down a little before taking a sip."

— Fiona Osgun, head of health information at Cancer Research UK

That advice fits what earlier evidence has long suggested: the risk is not a reason to give up tea or coffee, which contain bioactive compounds linked to health benefits. Multiple systematic reviews have reached similar conclusions — habitual consumption of very hot beverages is associated with higher esophageal cancer risk — while studies that directly measured temperatures found tea above 60°C carried significantly higher risk than cooled drinks.

Context and caveats

Esophageal SCC remains a relatively rare cancer — one analysis put the baseline risk at slightly more than one in 1,000 people, rising to about three in 1,000 among "very hot" drinkers. In the UK, where about 9,500 cases of esophageal cancer occur each year, researchers estimated that if the observed association reflects a true cause-and-effect relationship, about 14% of SCC cases — roughly 440 cases a year — could potentially be prevented if people drank beverages "hot" rather than "very hot."

The biggest ways to reduce risk of this cancer type remain not smoking and cutting down on alcohol, Cancer Research UK notes. But for the millions who drink their morning cuppa piping hot, the fix costs nothing: pour, wait, then sip.
